main.title: Final Fantasy Tactics
main.summary: Final Fantasy Tactics is a 1997 tactical role-playing game developed and published by Square for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: Ramza in the Lion War
cards.text: Final Fantasy Tactics is a 1997 tactical role-playing game developed and published by Square for the PlayStation. It was released in Japan in June 1997 and in North America in January 1998 by Sony Computer Entertainment. It is the first game of the Tactics sub-series within the Final Fantasy franchise, and the first entry set in the fictional world later known as Ivalice. The story follows Ramza Beoulve, a highborn cadet placed in the middle of a military conflict known as The Lion War, where two opposing noble factions are coveting the throne of the kingdom.

cards.heading: Matsuno's tactical vision of class conflict
cards.text: Production was begun in 1995 by Yasumi Matsuno, a newcomer who had created the Ogre Battle series at Quest Corporation. Matsuno's wish was for an accessible tactical game with a storyline focusing on class-based conflict and the rewriting of history. Matsuno acted as director and writer, Final Fantasy creator Hironobu Sakaguchi was producer, and the battles were designed by Hiroyuki Ito. Multiple other staff members were veterans of the Ogre Battle series, including artists Hiroshi Minagawa and Akihiko Yoshida, and composers Hitoshi Sakimoto and Masaharu Iwata. The game received critical acclaim and has become a cult classic since its release. The PlayStation version sold over one million units in Japan during 1997, and over 2.4 million worldwide by August 2011. It has been cited as one of the greatest video games of all time.

cards.heading: Ivalice and later editions
cards.text: The world of Ivalice became the setting for multiple other titles, including other Tactics games, and the 2006 mainline entry Final Fantasy XII. An enhanced port of the game, Final Fantasy Tactics: The War of the Lions, was released in 2007 as part of the Ivalice Alliance project. An expanded remaster for eighth and ninth generation consoles and Windows, subtitled The Ivalice Chronicles, was released on September 30, 2025.

main.title: Mischief Makers
main.subtitle: Grab first, ask later
main.summary: Mischief Makers is Treasure’s exuberant side-scrolling platform game for Nintendo 64. Marina Liteyears, a robotic maid, sets out to rescue her kidnapped creator, Professor Theo, on the planet Clancer. The adventure uses pre-rendered sprites and three-dimensional scenery, but its central idea is wonderfully physical: Marina can grab things, shake them and throw them. Enemies and objects become material for solving problems. Across five worlds and fifty-two stages, a small set of actions is repeatedly turned into a different kind of challenge.

cards.heading: Grab first, ask later
cards.text: Mischief Makers is Treasure’s exuberant side-scrolling platform game for Nintendo 64. Marina Liteyears, a robotic maid, sets out to rescue her kidnapped creator, Professor Theo, on the planet Clancer. The adventure uses pre-rendered sprites and three-dimensional scenery, but its central idea is wonderfully physical: Marina can grab things, shake them and throw them. Enemies and objects become material for solving problems. Across five worlds and fifty-two stages, a small set of actions is repeatedly turned into a different kind of challenge.

cards.heading: An object is an opportunity
cards.text: Picking something up rarely settles what to do with it. Shaking can reveal an item or change how an object works; throwing can clear a threat or provide a solution elsewhere. Marina’s movement adds running, jumping and directional boosts to the same toolkit. A scene that first resembles a conventional platform obstacle can therefore become a question about handling its contents. Treasure builds variety by changing the circumstances around these actions, allowing familiar controls to support races, encounters and more playful interruptions.

cards.heading: A reason to return
cards.text: Clearing a stage leaves room for a more demanding visit. Yellow gems reward additional discoveries and affect how much of the ending is shown, encouraging players to look beyond the immediate exit. The game’s character comes from this willingness to hide another use inside something already seen. Its expressive sprites and sudden changes of pace support the same idea: the world is available to be handled. Mischief Makers makes experimentation feel like part of Marina’s personality, rather than a separate layer of optional tasks.

main.title: Dungeon Keeper
main.summary: Dungeon Keeper is a strategy video game developed by Bullfrog Productions and published by Electronic Arts.

cards.text: Dungeon Keeper is a strategy video game developed by Bullfrog Productions and published by Electronic Arts. It was released on 27 June 1997 for MS-DOS and Windows 95. In Dungeon Keeper, the player builds and manages a dungeon, protecting it from invading "hero" characters intent on stealing its accumulated treasures, killing its monsters and ultimately destroying the keeper. The ultimate goal is to conquer the world by destroying the heroic forces and rival dungeon keepers in each realm. A character known as the Avatar (resembling the Avatar from Ultima VIII: Pagan) appears as the final hero. Dungeon Keeper uses Creative Technology's SoundFont technology to enhance its atmosphere. Multiplayer with up to four players is supported using a modem, or over a local network.

Dungeon Keeper took over two years to develop, and an expansion pack, a Direct3D version, and a level editor were released. Midway through development, lead developer Peter Molyneux decided to leave Bullfrog when the game was complete. Versions for the Sega Saturn and Sony PlayStation were in development, but cancelled. The game received critical acclaim, with reviewers praising the uniqueness and depth. Dungeon Keeper was re-released on GOG.com in 2011, Origin in 2016, and Steam in 2024. A fan-made mod, KeeperFX, was released, which fixes bugs and adds features. Dungeon Keeper was followed by a sequel, Dungeon Keeper 2, in 1999, and influenced games such as Lego Rock Raiders and Ghost Master.

main.title: Armored Core
main.subtitle: Build the machine before taking the contract
main.summary: Armored Core is FromSoftware's PlayStation mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 10 July 1997. In a future where humanity lives underground after a catastrophe, the player works as a mercenary pilot between competing corporate interests. The machine is assembled from interchangeable parts before being taken into missions. A successful contract pays for the next modification, linking combat to the workshop that precedes it. The series begins with that relationship: the player chooses what a machine can do, then discovers the consequences while trying to earn a living with it.

cards.heading: Build the machine before taking the contract
cards.text: Armored Core is FromSoftware's PlayStation mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 10 July 1997. In a future where humanity lives underground after a catastrophe, the player works as a mercenary pilot between competing corporate interests. The machine is assembled from interchangeable parts before being taken into missions. A successful contract pays for the next modification, linking combat to the workshop that precedes it. The series begins with that relationship: the player chooses what a machine can do, then discovers the consequences while trying to earn a living with it.

cards.heading: Every part changes the next decision
cards.text: Leg units, weapons and other components alter the performance of an Armored Core. A faster build can approach a battle differently from a heavily equipped one, making the garage a place to plan rather than merely decorate. Credits earned through missions allow more parts to be bought, opening new combinations as the campaign continues. The player must connect a machine's capabilities to the work ahead. An unsuccessful approach can suggest a change in equipment, giving preparation and execution a continuing influence on one another throughout the mercenary career.

cards.heading: The beginning of a long-running design
cards.text: Toshifumi Nabeshima directed the game, with mechanical designs by Shōji Kawamori and music by Keiichiro Segawa and Masaru Tateyama. Reviewers particularly welcomed the depth of customisation and the opportunity to fight another player. Two further PlayStation releases expanded the same foundation before Armored Core 2 moved the series to PlayStation 2. The original establishes many of its recurring concerns: corporate power, paid combat and a pilot whose choices are expressed through machinery. Its workshop gives those ideas a practical form that the player handles before every sortie.

main.title: Bulk Slash
main.subtitle: A machine with two ways to fight
main.summary: Bulk Slash is CAProduction's transforming-mech action game, released by Hudson Soft for Saturn in Japan on 11 July 1997.

cards.heading: A machine with two ways to fight
cards.text: Bulk Slash is CAProduction's transforming-mech action game, released by Hudson Soft for Saturn in Japan on 11 July 1997. Pilot Cress Dawley fights a futuristic war across seven stages, switching his machine between ground combat and flight. Missions give the player objectives to pursue before confronting a boss. The transformation makes the environment useful in two different ways: a place to maneuver and fight on foot becomes airspace to cross, with weapons and movement changing alongside the machine's shape.

cards.heading: A navigator changes the mission
cards.text: Hidden navigators can be found during the stages and recruited through the Manageable Intelligent Support System, abbreviated M.I.S.S. Each brings particular support abilities, and the selected companion gains experience separately from the player's score. Returning with that navigator develops the relationship and can alter the ending. The player therefore has another reason to explore a stage beyond its immediate military objective. Between missions, choosing a companion becomes part of preparing the next sortie, connecting the action to a growing supporting cast.

cards.heading: Saturn action with a transforming center
cards.text: CAProduction had previously worked on Hagane and Sapphire, bringing experience in fast action to Saturn's three-dimensional spaces. Takeshi Sato composed the soundtrack. The game remained a Japanese release, with an English fan translation arriving in 2021. Its identity rests on the connection between a freely moving combat machine and the navigator beside its pilot. Learning a mission means understanding which form works best in a space, while further visits can uncover another companion and another reason to follow the route again.

main.title: SaGa Frontier
main.subtitle: Seven protagonists explore the Regions
main.summary: On July 11, 1997 Square released SaGa Frontier for PlayStation in Japan.

cards.heading: Different routes through the same worlds
cards.text: Square released SaGa Frontier for PlayStation in Japan on July 11, 1997. Seven protagonists begin different stories across the Regions, places with their own cultures, technology and magic. Nonlinear progression lets players try different routes and party combinations. Its linked-technique combo system also expands turn-based battles, joining actions into stronger attacks when the conditions are right.

cards.heading: Seven paths through the Regions
cards.text: SaGa Frontier's Free Scenario System offers seven protagonists sharing The Regions, worlds connected by regular ships but differing in culture, technology and magic. Each character has a main story, yet many routes remain open from the beginning. Talking to people can reveal information, recruit companions or start an optional quest. Encounters between protagonists make one journey touch another. The chosen character, party members and earlier decisions can change events, so exploring a familiar place with a different lead may uncover another part of its story.

cards.heading: Learning skills and combining attacks
cards.text: Players encounter groups of enemies on the field screen, upon which they switch to the battle screen. The battle screen depicts 2D-animated sprites amidst a 3D-rotating background. Battles are turn-based; the player chooses the characters' actions and must allow them, along with those of the enemies, to play out. A variety of weapons, special skills, and magic spells are at the player's disposal. Most skills are learned mid-battle, while many spells are purchased in the game's shops. If certain conditions are met within the battle, party members on either side can create combination attacks for added damage. Winning battles increases player character statistics such as hit points (HP), life points (LP), strength, and quickness. Outside of combat, players can equip and unequip (or "seal") weapons, armor, skills, spells, and items. First introduced in the Game Boy incarnations of the SaGa series, the game contains different races that exist within the Regions: the Humans, the Mystics, the Half-Mystics (half Human and half Mystic), Monsters, and the Mecs (robots).

cards.heading: Bonuses for completing each scenario
cards.text: The player is encouraged to complete each of the seven scenarios one after the other. For added incentive, beating a character's game and saving its completion to the system data adds some bonuses. After beating one character's game, essentially every character in the following game starts off stronger and with better gear than before, and may depend on how many battles players fought in their previous quest that they saved on the system data. Fulfilling all seven main quests allows the player access to the "2nd Division" room, in which the player can fight all final bosses and talk to the game's programmers.

main.title: Ghost in the Shell
main.subtitle: Section 9 recruits a different viewpoint
main.summary: Ghost in the Shell is Exact's PlayStation action game, first released in Japan on 17 July 1997. The player joins Public Security Section 9 as a recruit piloting a Fuchikoma, a small robotic combat vehicle. Missions follow an investigation into the Human Liberation Front, placing the action within the world of Masamune Shirow's manga. The vehicle changes how that world is explored: walls and ceilings become surfaces to travel across. Rather than following a human figure through corridors, the player learns to read a room as a machine capable of climbing it.

cards.heading: Section 9 recruits a different viewpoint
cards.text: Ghost in the Shell is Exact's PlayStation action game, first released in Japan on 17 July 1997. The player joins Public Security Section 9 as a recruit piloting a Fuchikoma, a small robotic combat vehicle. Missions follow an investigation into the Human Liberation Front, placing the action within the world of Masamune Shirow's manga. The vehicle changes how that world is explored: walls and ceilings become surfaces to travel across. Rather than following a human figure through corridors, the player learns to read a room as a machine capable of climbing it.

cards.heading: The wall becomes another floor
cards.text: The Fuchikoma can move from the ground onto vertical surfaces and overhead structures, allowing the player to approach enemies from unusual positions. A route that appears closed at floor level may remain open above it. Combat therefore asks for awareness of the whole space, not only the ground ahead. Learning how the view changes during a climb is part of gaining control. The movement gives the game its particular character, turning architecture into a choice of firing positions and making the player's route an active part of an encounter.

cards.heading: A collaboration between manga and games
cards.text: Shirow supplied character and mechanical designs, while Production I.G. worked with Exact on the production. Animated sequences connect the missions to the cast around Section 9, and the English release uses the voice cast familiar from the 1995 film's English dub. The game itself draws its setting and tone from the manga rather than continuing that film. Its electronic soundtrack received an album release alongside other supporting material. Reviewers praised the animation, music and climbing mechanics, helping establish it as a distinctive adaptation within the PlayStation's early three-dimensional library.

main.title: Real Sound: Kaze no Regret
main.subtitle: An adventure experienced through sound
main.summary: On July 18, 1997 Warp released Real Sound: Kaze no Regret for Sega Saturn in Japan.

cards.heading: Listening becomes the centre of play
cards.text: On July 18, 1997 Warp released Real Sound: Kaze no Regret for Sega Saturn in Japan. Kenji Eno built an audio adventure in which the screen remains essentially without imagery and the story is followed through voices, music, sound and cues marking moments of choice. The idea also grew from the desire to create an experience accessible to blind and sighted players on equal terms. Voices and sound cues carry the information needed to follow the story and make choices.

cards.heading: An audio adventure played with a blank screen
cards.text: Real Sound is an audio game that plays similarly to a visual novel. The screen is blank throughout the duration of the game, and the player spends the majority of the time listening as the plot unfolds.

cards.heading: Chimes announce a choice that changes the story
cards.text: However, at critical points in the story a set of chimes will ring, signifying that the player needs to make a decision at that moment. These choices impact how the story progresses. The Dreamcast version features an optional "visual mode", which displays non-essential still pictures on the screen.

cards.heading: Blind players’ letters and a promise of donated Saturns
cards.text: Kenji Eno conceived Real Sound after receiving letters from blind fans in Japan. He wanted blind and sighted players to experience the same game. When Sega sought exclusive rights, he required the company to donate a thousand Saturn consoles to visually impaired people, with Warp supplying copies of the game. Eno later cited that agreement when explaining why he had kept Real Sound tied to its original platform arrangement.

main.title: The King of Fighters '97
main.summary: The King of Fighters '97, often shortened as KOF '97, is a 1997 fighting video game developed and published by SNK for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms.

cards.text: The King of Fighters '97, often shortened as KOF '97, is a 1997 fighting video game developed and published by SNK for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms. It is the fourth game in The King of Fighters (KOF) series. The game was ported to the Neo Geo CD console and released worldwide; it was also ported to the PlayStation and Sega Saturn consoles in Japan. KOF '97 is the last game in the "Orochi Saga" storyline, which began in The King of Fighters '95. The new tournament focuses on the servants of the demon Yamata no Orochi, also known as the "Will of Gaia", who plan to revive their master by gathering energy and sacrifices from the fighters in the KOF tournament.

KOF '97 is the first game in the series to be directed by its battle system designer Toyohisa Tanabe. The original director is credited to Masanori Kuwasashi, who stopped working on the series after The King of Fighters '96. The creation of the game's characters primarily focused on creating bosses, especially Orochi, to properly tell the game's story in an appealing fashion. Among its several ports, SNK developed a version of KOF '97 subtitled Global Match that has online features.

KOF '97 received the 1997 Gamest award for Best Direction. Critics were divided on whether its controls and balance improved on previous instalments. The game sold well and was followed by The King of Fighters '98, which includes most of the Orochi arc cast, who fight in a non-canonical tournament. Yumekobo also created a visual novel with role-playing game elements titled The King of Fighters: Kyo, which retells the events of The King of Fighters '97 but primarily focuses on Kyo's life. The first handheld-based game in the series, King of Fighters R-1, was released in 1998 based on The King of Fighters '97. A spin-off light novel titled The King of Fantasy was released in 2019. The combined ports sold together over 336,000 copies in Japan.

main.title: Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon
main.subtitle: Konami · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon is Konami's Nintendo 64 action adventure about preventing the Peach Mountain Shoguns from transforming Japan into a giant theatrical production. Goemon travels with Ebisumaru, Sasuke and Yae through towns, open country and dungeons, switching between companions to use their different abilities. Traditional imagery sits beside machinery, sudden musical performances and deliberately absurd humour. The journey makes the group's personalities part of its geography: a place that stops one traveller may be crossed by another who has learned the right technique.

cards.heading: Four travellers in a very strange Japan
cards.text: Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon is Konami's Nintendo 64 action adventure about preventing the Peach Mountain Shoguns from transforming Japan into a giant theatrical production. Goemon travels with Ebisumaru, Sasuke and Yae through towns, open country and dungeons, switching between companions to use their different abilities. Traditional imagery sits beside machinery, sudden musical performances and deliberately absurd humour. The journey makes the group's personalities part of its geography: a place that stops one traveller may be crossed by another who has learned the right technique.

cards.heading: Learn the ability, remember the obstacle
cards.text: Ebisumaru can shrink to pass through small openings, while the other companions bring their own weapons and special movements. Training challenges introduce abilities that open further routes, encouraging the player to connect a new skill with a place seen earlier. Towns provide conversation, equipment and a pause between expeditions. Their inhabitants give the adventure a social rhythm alongside its platforming and fighting. Moving onward involves understanding what a companion can do as well as learning where the next important destination lies.

cards.heading: A robot battle changes the scale
cards.text: Major confrontations place the player inside the enormous Impact robot, shifting the view and controls for a much larger fight. Those sequences and the extravagant songs make the adventure's changes of tone part of its identity. Released in Japan in 1997 and overseas in 1998, it introduced many Western players to a broader version of Goemon's world. The game treats its setting as a place where everyday travel, supernatural abilities and giant machinery can belong to the same expedition without losing the comic company at its centre.
